d.title: The 7% of the definition that decides everything
d.caption: This split is the whole lesson. When a tool is not being called, people edit the **schema**, because that is where the substance appears to be — and the schema has no influence on selection at all, since it is read *after* the model has decided. Selection is the name and the description, which together are a fraction of the tokens: the description is **6 of 84**. It is a retrieval problem, and the description is the document.

d.title: The audience for a description is the model, not a maintainer
d.caption: "Calls the v2 weather API with a 5-second timeout" is true, costs tokens on every request, and has **no bearing on whether the model should select it**. A description's only job is to separate this tool from the others it sits beside, so write what distinguishes it — when to reach for it, and when not to — and put the implementation notes in a comment where they cost nothing.

nodes.label: Billed on every request
nodes.sub: for information the model cannot use

d.title: Once selected, arguments are a structured-output problem
d.caption: Everything from 1.8 and 2.7 applies unchanged, with one addition that is specific to tools: a per-property `description` is **a prompt sitting exactly where the value is generated**, which is the closest thing in the API to an instruction with a guaranteed location. An `enum` is a hard constraint; a property description is a soft one at the right place.

nodes.label: A property description
nodes.sub: a prompt at the generation point

d.title: Three of these have a reliable version; one genuinely is prompting
d.caption: `tool_choice` is the only reliable way to control selection — everything else is **influence, and influence is a distribution**. The practical consequence is pipeline-shaped: if your agent always searches before answering, that is not an instruction, it is step one, and forcing it costs nothing while removing a failure mode. Save `"auto"` for turns where there is a genuine decision. The last row is the one with no mechanical answer.

d.title: The quality argument arrives before the cost argument
d.caption: 1.9 measured the cost at 85 tokens per definition re-sent every turn, with routing crossing over around six tools. But **selection degrades before the bill does**: tools with overlapping descriptions compete, and the model's job is a retrieval task that gets harder with every near-duplicate you add. So the first fix is never 'attach fewer tools to save money' — it is to make the descriptions separate, and only then to route.

d.title: A signature is a typed interface; the prompt is generated from it
d.caption: The change is in **what you write down**. Instead of a string containing instructions and format directions, you declare input fields, output fields and a docstring, and the framework builds the prompt. Unusually for this area you can look at the result without spending anything — the adapter is an ordinary object — and what it produces is a `[[ ## field ## ]]` delimiter scheme with the docstring as the objective.

nodes.label: So you can review what is sent
nodes.sub: which is the thing to do first

d.title: What each optimiser actually searches
d.caption: `BootstrapFewShot` does something much narrower than "optimise the prompt", and knowing what makes the whole thing less mysterious: it runs the module on training inputs, keeps the traces the metric scored as correct, and uses those as demonstrations. **It is automated example selection** — 2.2's work, done by machine. Instruction search is a different optimiser and a much larger compute bill.

cells.text: a larger set, far more compute

d.title: The four claims, graded
d.caption: Two hold outright, two with caveats. **Portability is the strongest** and the one worth dwelling on: a hand-tuned prompt is tuned against one model's quirks — the chat template it expects, how literally it takes an instruction, whether it responds to XML tags — and a signature has none of that baked in, because the prompt is produced at call time by an adapter that knows the target. Modularity is the most underrated: a typed interface makes a chain composition rather than string concatenation.
cells: a chain becomes composition, not concatenation
it swaps prompt tuning for metric tuning
the strongest claim - no quirks baked in

d.title: Compiling is an API bill before anything is deployed
d.caption: The cost that is easy to miss: compiling runs the module over the training set, sometimes many times, and those are **real API calls**. `MIPROv2` on a few hundred examples is a meaningful bill paid before a single user sees the feature — worth budgeting deliberately rather than discovering on an invoice. Which also sets the threshold for when the setup is worth it: a prompt you will tune once does not repay it, and a module you will port across three models does.

nodes.label: A bill before deployment

nodes.label: And you need the metric either way

d.title: "Representative" is the word doing the work
d.caption: 30–50 representative inputs is the usual suggestion, and *representative* gets read as *typical* — which produces a set every candidate passes and therefore **a measurement that cannot discriminate**. A set that can tell candidates apart is deliberately unbalanced toward the cases that break things: known production failures are 20% of it, and cases where the correct behaviour is to decline are 10%, because nothing else measures whether a prompt knows its limits.

cells.text: everything that has broken in production
the right answer is to decline

d.title: Every metric is blind to something; know which thing
d.caption: The practical rule is to **prefer a cheap deterministic metric wherever one exists** — an exact-match check on an extracted field costs nothing, is perfectly reproducible and cannot drift. Reach for a judge only when the output is genuinely open-ended, and then treat the judge as a component that needs its own evaluation, because it is one. Note the third row: schema validity is usually the only half collected, and it is the half that tells you least.
cells: which class is failing, unless sliced
whether the value is in the source

d.title: What a test set of that size can actually detect
d.caption: At 95% confidence and 80% power, detecting a **2-point** lift from a 0.85 baseline needs 4,724 cases. 30 to 50 is nowhere near that, and the honest reading is at the bottom: n=30 detects a lift of roughly 50 points, n=50 about 15, n=100 about 11.5. So a 30-case set is not a measurement of small improvements — it is a smoke test, which is a useful thing to own as long as you do not read percentages off it.

d.title: A three-point improvement is not significant at any size you will run
d.caption: 0.82 against 0.85 — a difference people ship on — fails significance at 50 cases, at 200, and **at 1,000**, where p is still 0.0805. This is the number to keep in mind every time a prompt change moves a small test set by a few points: the move is almost certainly noise, and the correct response is not to run it again hoping for a better draw. Either get a much larger set, or accept that the two candidates are indistinguishable and choose on another ground.

d.title: Offline rejects; production chooses
d.caption: What production adds is **real inputs and real outcomes**. An offline set measures whether the output matched what you expected; production measures whether users accepted it, edited it, retried or escalated — and no offline metric substitutes for those. What production costs is time and exposure: half your users get the worse variant until you stop. Which is the argument for both, in that order: offline to reject what is clearly worse, an A/B to choose between the survivors.
